dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Anita. Good morning, how can I help you?
Yeah, so the fellow came out Friday and gave me the quote, and now I don't know if I should sign it. Is this the right office?
Okay, I might be missing the start of that. Which quote, and what kind of work are we talking about?
Oh. The fence. I'm sorry, I figured it was on there already. A fence company, they want to put in a fence around the back yard, and I want to check before I sign anything.
No problem, that makes sense. You're smart to check first. Can I get your name and the address where the fence would go?
Alan Gardiner. It's 331 Admiral Kalbfus Road, up in the North End.
Thank you, Mr. Gardiner. And you're on speakerphone, I think? You sound a little far away.
Yeah, I've got the phone on the table, my hands are full of papers. Can you hear me alright?
I can hear you fine. Go ahead. What kind of fence are you planning?
Vinyl. White vinyl. And, um, whatever is allowed tall. I'd like it as tall as they let me.
Okay. So the main thing you're asking is whether you need a permit for it?
Yes, that's it. Do I need a permit? The salesman said the company handles all that, or maybe he said I handle it. I wasn't sure which. He was talking pretty fast.

Generally, yes, a fence in the city does need a permit, and the rules depend on things like height and where on the property it sits. As for who files it, that's often something the contractor does, but it should be written in your contract so you know.
Written in the contract. Okay. So it's not the same as, say, a shed? I thought you only need paperwork for a building.
A fence is treated separately from a shed, but it still usually needs approval before it goes up. It's not just for buildings.
Huh. Alright. And the height. Is it six feet, or is that the front, or the back? I read something online and it said four in one place and six in another.
That's probably what you saw, yes. There are usually different limits for the front of a property and the back or sides. Is the fence going across the front, or just around the back yard?
Just the back. Well, it goes along the side a ways too. Down the side to the corner of the house. Is that the front or the back?

That's a good question, and it's exactly why I'd ask about it. The part along the side that runs toward the street can be treated differently from the part behind the house. Is your lot a corner lot, or does it have neighbors on both sides?
Neighbors both sides. One of them has a chain link already. Is that a problem?
No, that's not a problem. But where the line sits matters. Do you know where your property line is? Do you have a survey or plot plan?
A survey. Hmm. I think I've got something from when I bought the house, but that was a long time ago. Would that be the one with the little drawing of the lot?

Yes, that's the one. A drawing of the lot with the measurements. If you can find it, bring it or have the fence company use it. The permit application will generally want to know where the fence is going.
Okay. So the company would use that. Or I would. I'll have to ask him who does that part.
Right. Ask him directly, and ask that it's in writing. Some homeowners are surprised after the fact.
Now, the fee. What does it cost to get the permit? Because it's not on his quote, and I want to know if that's extra on top.

I don't have the exact fee in front of me, and it can depend on the project, so I don't want to give you a number that's off. What I can do is transfer you to the permit desk, or you can check with them when you apply. But yes, the permit fee is normally separate from what the contractor charges for the fence.
Separate. So if his quote says nothing about it, it's probably extra.
Possibly, unless he says he's including it. That's another reason to ask. A line on the quote that says permit included, or not included, would clear it up.
Good idea. See, I'm a careful shopper. I check the unit prices, the price per foot, all of that. I had three quotes and this one's the cheapest per foot, but if the permit's extra, maybe it's not.
That's a smart way to compare. Make sure each quote is counting the same things, the gates, the posts, removal of anything old, and the permit. Then you're comparing apples to apples.
Right, right. The other two, I think, had the permit in. I'd have to look. He had a gate on there, I remember that. Is a gate different?
A gate is normally part of the same fence application. You wouldn't need a separate permit for it, but it should be shown on what you submit.
Okay. So one application. Um, what about, if I put it up and don't get the permit, what happens? Hypothetically.
Hypothetically, the city can require you to apply after the fact, or to change or remove it if it doesn't meet the rules. That's a lot more trouble and expense than just doing it right at the start.
Yeah, no, I don't want that. I'm not going to do that. I just want to know what I'm signing. So, wait, you said four feet in the front. Did you say that?
I said there are typically different limits for front and back, but I'd rather the permit desk confirm the exact heights for your lot. I don't want you to order six-foot panels based on my memory.
No, no, that's fair. So I should hold off on signing.
I'd say hold off until you've confirmed who pulls the permit, what the fee is, and what height you're allowed along that side. Then sign with those answers on paper.
Alright. Can you transfer me to the permit desk, then?
I can. They may be at lunch since it's right around noon. If nobody picks up, I can take your number and have someone call you back. Is the number you're on now the best one?
It's 401-555-0163. That's the house phone, but I'm always around.
Got it, 401-555-0163. And that's Alan Gardiner, 331 Admiral Kalbfus Road, asking about a vinyl back yard fence, permit requirement, fee, and allowed height. Did I get that right?
That's right. Vinyl. And the side part, whether it counts as front. Don't forget that part.
I'll add the side question. I'll note it so you don't have to explain it all again. They should reach out today or first thing tomorrow, with the holiday week coming.
Oh, that's right, it's almost Christmas. Okay. So I'll wait to hear, and I won't sign anything until then.
That sounds like a good plan. And if you find that survey, keep it handy.
I'll look in the hall closet. Thank you, uh, Anita, was it?
Yes, Anita. You're welcome, Mr. Gardiner. Take care.
Okay. Thanks. Bye now.
